title: The night watch on the Ganga
hookLine: two men keep watch by a fire all night, and at dawn two princes twist their hair into a vow
carry: jata: a vow you can see
last: SAKHYA: LOVING GOD AS A FRIEND.

lines: A LOW FIRE, A BOW ACROSS THE KNEES.
cards: The fire is low. Rama and Sita sleep on a bed of grass under a tree, a few feet away. Lakshmana sits up with his bow across his knees, wide awake.
Guha comes and sits beside him. Late at night, beside someone outside the family, with the people you love asleep nearby, things get said that daylight keeps in.
That's what happens on this riverbank before the night is out.

teach.h: GO AND SLEEP. HOW CAN I SLEEP?
teach.b: Guha speaks first, kindly. I've made a bed for you. Go and sleep.
My people and I will keep watch; we know this forest. Lakshmana says no. How can I sleep, when my brother, who should be lying in a palace, is lying on the ground?

Then he says out loud what he's carried all day: the old king, who he thinks won't survive the grief; the mothers, alone in the palace; the city, emptied of joy. Guha listens, and Valmiki says Guha weeps too.
Two men, one grief. In the morning, Rama sends Sumantra home with the empty chariot, to comfort the king.
Then he asks Guha for the milky sap of a banyan tree, and with it he and Lakshmana mat their hair into jata, the coils forest ascetics wear. Here's the teaching in that sap.

Matted hair isn't a costume. It's a vow you can see. Forest ascetics stop caring for their hair as a sign they've left the palace behind, and Shiva himself is pictured with jata, the river Ganga caught in his locks.

teach.h: A VOW MARKED ON THE BODY.
teach.b: Hindus still mark a vow on the body.

teach.h: JATA: A VOW YOU CAN SEE.
teach.b: Many devotees offer their hair at the temple at Tirupati when a prayer is answered; some sadhus keep jata for life; and many families shave a child's first hair as an offering.
When Rama twists banyan sap into his hair, he's saying with his whole head: I meant it. Now the only ones left are Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and a friend with a boat.

how: Matted hair, jata, is worn by some Hindu ascetics as a sign of renunciation; many devotees offer their hair at temples such as Tirumala (Tirupati) to fulfill a vow.

o: the bark clothing worn by those who renounce
the matted coils of hair forest ascetics wear
a sacred thread tied on the arm for protection

games.q: the night watch — tap the pairs.
p: offers to keep watch so Lakshmana can sleep
a forest vow worn on the head

s: Lakshmana sleeps while Guha keeps watch
he refuses to sleep while his brother lies on the ground.
Guha weeps with Lakshmana through the night
two men, one grief, through one night.
the matted hair was a disguise for the road
jata is the sign of a forest vow; Shiva himself is pictured wearing it.

games.q: you're Rama at dawn on the Ganga. you've vowed fourteen years as a forest ascetic. how do you show it?
o: keep your palace hair; a vow is private.
mat your hair into jata with banyan sap.
wear your crown until the forest.
games.why: he and Lakshmana take on jata, the matted hair of ascetics: the vow made visible, the way Hindus still mark a vow on the body.

practice: Many Hindus keep a vrata, a small vow, for a day or a season: a fast on Mondays, a prayer each morning. If you pray, choose one small vow for this week and offer it silently. If you don't, choose one small promise to yourself.
Then breathe with it, and notice where in your body you'd carry it.

wordCard.voice: Jata, the matted coils forest ascetics wear. Guha keeps watch beside Lakshmana and weeps with him, and at dawn Rama and Lakshmana take on jata: the vow made visible.

orig.note: Sanskrit jaṭā: matted hair, the coils worn by forest ascetics; Rama and Lakshmana take it on at the Ganga.

carryVoice: Your line: jata: a vow you can see. Tomorrow, the boat and the river. That's day five hundred thirty-five.
